_comment: The bibliography behind the library. TWO KINDS OF RECORD: the sources behind a citation in core.json, and the field's standard reading, which carries `generalReading: true`. The flag is ADDITIVE and not a category -- it says a record earns its place on its own, and says nothing about whether anything cites it, so a record may be both. Modelling it as a two-value role would force a choice that does not exist, and the first time a general-reading record acquired a citation somebody would have to decide which list it leaves. A general-reading record meets every rule a cited one does: identifier, title, authors, year, namespace, no duplicates -- it is a different reason to be here, not a lower standard. A record that is neither cited nor flagged raises `referenceOrphan` in the health list, which is a question rather than a fault: cite it, flag it, or remove it. The pack stores an identifier; this stores what the identifier IS, so a reader can see the paper without leaving the app. Every record here was resolved against CrossRef (or PubMed, or arXiv, or a library catalogue) and its title, journal or publisher, authors and year read off that record -- nothing is recalled, and nothing is added from a reference list without resolving it first. `year` is the issue year, which is what a reader will match against; several of these were online-first the year before. A record carries a `doi`, a `pmid` OR an `isbn`: some journals issue no DOI at all, and most golf coaching doctrine was never published in a journal in the first place -- it lives in books and in chapters of edited volumes, whose identifier is an ISBN. Refusing any of the three would mean the pack could cite a source no reader could ever be shown. AN ISBN-ONLY RECORD CANNOT BACK `supported` OR `established`: a book is not peer review, those two tiers mean a peer-reviewed source tested the named pair and that independent sources reproduced it, and the pack loader demotes any claim that tries. A book belongs at `practice` or `indirect`, which is not a lesser status -- it is what lets 'the field agrees but has never measured it' finally say who the field is. NO commercial organisation, product or certification body may be named in this file: core_pack_test greps content bytes for it, and two of these papers have manufacturer-employed authors -- they are peer-reviewed with DOIs, and only the work is recorded.

references.title: Low Back Pain in Professional Golfers: The Role of Associated Hip and Low Back Range-of-Motion Deficits
references.authors: Vad, Bhat, Basrai, Gebeh, Aspergren, Andrews
references.journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
references.establishes: In 42 male professional golfers, a history of low back pain correlated with decreased LEAD hip internal rotation, FABERE distance and lumbar extension. No significant trail-hip finding — the asymmetry is the result.

references.title: Lumbopelvic kinematic characteristics of golfers with limited hip rotation
references.journal: The American Journal of Sports Medicine
references.establishes: Golfers with hip internal rotation below 20° showed significantly greater lumbar flexion, axial rotation and lateral bending, and greater pelvic posterior tilt, than those at or above 30°.

references.title: Kinematic relationship between rotation of lumbar spine and hip joints during golf swing in professional golfers
references.establishes: Lumbar–hip rotational coupling of r≈0.81. The lead hip's contribution to overall rotation is markedly high in the EARLY downswing; the lumbar spine contributes more late.

references.title: The Biomechanics of the Modern Golf Swing: Implications for Lower Back Injuries
references.establishes: Review. Skilled golfers laterally slide the pelvis toward the target and this contributes to clubhead speed; argues the lumbar spine may not safely accommodate the resulting loads.

references.title: Low back pain and golf: A review of biomechanical risk factors
references.establishes: Professionals with low back pain show significantly more lead-side lateral bending in the backswing. Notes that crunch-factor evidence is conflicting and was not reproduced as a risk factor by two independent methods.

references.title: Biomechanical parameters of the golf swing associated with lower back pain: A systematic review
references.authors: Watson, Coughlan, Clement, Murray, Murray, Miller
references.establishes: Mixed and null results: NO significant differences in hip angle, trunk angle or crunch factor in recreational golfers. Elite golfers with low back pain showed shorter transition phases and greater peak lead-side lumbar lateral flexion. Nothing cites it, and it is the most load-bearing uncited paper here: it is the reason every injury note in the library is phrased as an association with stated uncertainty rather than as a risk, and no note may be strengthened past what it supports.

references.title: The role of upper torso and pelvis rotation in driving performance during the golf swing
references.authors: Myers, Lephart, Tsai, Sell, Smoliga, Jolly
references.establishes: X-factor and upper-torso rotational velocity are significantly related to ball velocity. Read alongside Madrid et al. 2020, which disagrees.

references.title: The relationship between biomechanical variables and driving performance during the golf swing
references.establishes: Models accounted for 44–74% of ball-velocity variance. X-factor, delayed release of the arms and wrists, trunk tilting and weight shifting were significantly related to ball velocity. Read alongside Madrid et al. 2020, which disagrees on wrist release.

references.title: Elite golfers' kinematic sequence in full-swing and partial-swing shots
references.establishes: Significant proximal-to-distal temporal sequencing with a successive increase in peak segment angular speed — across genders, skill levels, and both full and partial shots.

references.title: Rotational Biomechanics of the Elite Golf Swing: Benchmarks for Amateurs
references.authors: Meister, Ladd, Butler, Zhao, Rogers, Ray, Rose
references.establishes: 10 professional and 5 amateur male golfers. Benchmark curves for pelvic rotation, upper-torso rotation and X-factor across the whole swing. In professionals, peak free moment per kilogram, peak X-factor and peak S-factor were highly consistent — coefficients of variation 6.8%, 7.4% and 8.4%. The downswing was initiated by reversal of pelvic rotation followed by reversal of upper-torso rotation, and peak X-factor preceded peak free moment in every swing of every golfer, occurring during the initial downswing. For amateurs, the number of factors falling outside one to two standard deviations of the professional means increased with handicap.

references.title: Golf Swing Rotational Velocity: The Essential Follow-Through
references.authors: Steele, Roh, Mahtani, Meister, Ladd, Rose
references.establishes: 11 professionals compared with 5 amateurs. Rotational velocities were highly consistent in professionals through the downswing — coefficients of variation 0.086 for upper torso and 0.079 for pelvis. Peak upper-torso rotational velocity and peak X-prime occurred AFTER impact, in the follow-through, while peak pelvic rotational velocity occurred during the downswing. Pelvic velocity at impact was reduced in amateurs compared with professionals (p=0.019).

references.title: The swing performance Index: Developing a single-score index of golf swing rotational biomechanics quantified with 3D kinematics
references.journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
references.establishes: Builds a single-score index on the professional benchmark curves, over 11 professionals and 5 amateurs spanning handicap 4 to novice. The selected formula combines three variables: peak pelvic rotational velocity before impact, pelvic rotational velocity AT IMPACT, and peak upper-torso rotational velocity after impact. Professionals standardise to 100 ± 10; amateurs average 82 ± 4. Independent support that pelvic rotational velocity at impact carries skill information.

references.title: Association between the On-Plane Angular Motions of the Axle-Chain System and Clubhead Speed in Skilled Male Golfers
references.authors: Madrid, Avalos, Levine, Tuttle, Becker, Kwon
references.establishes: 66 skilled golfers. Higher clubhead speed was associated with shorter downswings, larger rotation ranges, larger hip–shoulder separation at impact and delayed transitions — but clubhead speed was NOT well associated with wrist-cock angles or ranges, or with X-factor and X-factor stretch. This is the conflicting half of the wrist-release and X-factor claims; it is recorded here because it must be read, not because anything cites it.

references.title: Effects of on-plane wrist release style on morphological, temporal, and kinematic swing characteristic in golf drives performed by skilled male golfers
references.authors: Cheng, Mori, Lee, Martinez, Baek, Alvis, Kwon
references.establishes: 84 elite male golfers across four wrist-release styles. Delayed-release styles showed larger uncocking velocities, longer transitions, shorter early-downswing phases and a complete proximal-to-distal sequence, compared with early-release and recocking styles.

references.title: The Influence of Face Angle and Club Path on the Resultant Launch Angle of a Golf Ball
references.journal: Proceedings of the 12th Conference of the International Sports Engineering Association
references.establishes: Player and robot studies: initial launch direction falls 61–83% toward the face angle, with the remainder toward the club path, varying by club type.

references.title: The Role of Friction and Tangential Compliance on the Resultant Launch Angle of a Golf Ball
references.journal: Proceedings of the 13th Conference of the International Sports Engineering Association
references.establishes: A Hertzian impact model with tangential compliance via Coulomb friction predicts launch direction from delivered face angle and path, and explores launch direction against the friction coefficient.

references.title: The physics of golf
references.establishes: Peer-reviewed physics review: double-pendulum swing models, club–ball impact, the loft / launch / spin relationships, and turf interaction. The general impact physics behind most of the strike and ball-flight edges.

references.title: Small changes in ball position at address cause a chain effect in golf swing
references.authors: Kim, Lee, Lee, Lee, Shim, Lee
references.establishes: 20 professionals, five mediolateral ball positions, SPM analysis. Target-side ball position produced a significantly more open shoulder angle at address, during the downswing and at impact, plus lead-foot weight bias — and a less in-to-out club path at impact. The trend reversed for trail-side positions.

references.title: Biomechanical Effects of Ball Position on Address Position Variables of Elite Golfers
references.authors: Kim, Koh, Cho, Lee, Lee, Lee
references.journal: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine
references.establishes: 11 male professional golfers, 3D motion analysis with eight infrared cameras and two force platforms, eight ball positions in the mediolateral and anteroposterior directions. Moving the ball mediolaterally significantly changed shoulder rotation and club-face aim at address and the vertical ground reaction force under the lead foot; at impact it significantly changed club-face aim, club path and angle of attack. The companion to Kim et al. 2021 — that one measures the address end, this one the delivery end. This journal issues no DOI, so the PMID is the identifier.

references.title: Towards a Biomechanical Understanding of Tempo in the Golf Swing
references.establishes: PREPRINT, not peer reviewed, and listed here for attribution rather than support. Models the body/club system as a simple harmonic oscillator — a biomechanical clock — accounting for total swing duration, the ratio of backswing to downswing time, and tempo's relative insensitivity to shot length. Shaft-mounted accelerometers at roughly 250 Hz, ten to twenty five-iron swings each, over 12 playing professionals, 13 teaching professionals and good amateurs, and 18 other golfers. The backswing:downswing ratio is centred at 3.0 in all three groups; playing professionals span 2.5 to 3.5 with very small per-golfer standard deviation and swing uniformly faster than the rest. This is the source of the widely quoted 3:1 figure. NOTE THE BASIS: their backswing is measured from the START OF MOTION, not from address, so it is not the same quantity this product's tempo ratio reports.

references.title: The role of biomechanics in maximising distance and accuracy of golf shots
references.establishes: The field's standard review of the biomechanics of distance and accuracy. Here as general reading rather than in support of a claim — it is the survey a reader should find first, and it will pick up citations as the pack matures, which is exactly the overlap the additive flag exists to allow.

references.title: The importance of stretching the X-Factor in the golf downswing
references.establishes: X-Factor Stretch. A chapter in the edited volume 'Optimising Performance in Golf' (P. Thomas, ed.), pp. 192-199; the ISBN identifies that volume. Establishes that pelvis-thorax separation does not peak at the top of the backswing: it INCREASES during the early downswing, beyond its value at the top, and it does so for skilled and less-skilled golfers alike. The increase is larger in the more skilled group. The conclusion drawn is that the stretch matters more than the separation measured at the top, which is why a measurement taken at the top alone can miss the quantity that discriminates. FIGURES NOT RECORDED: the chapter's F statistics, p values and per-group percentages could not be resolved against the source when this record was filed, and are deliberately absent rather than transcribed from a secondary quotation. The qualitative finding above is what this record supports; anyone needing the numbers must read the chapter and add them here.

references.title: Golf Swing Biomechanics: A Systematic Review and Methodological Recommendations for Kinematics
references.establishes: The map of the field, over 92 articles, organised into the five domains this library also works in: X-factor, crunch factor, swing plane and clubhead trajectory, kinematic sequence, and joint angular kinematics. Its most useful finding for us is a negative one: the LACK OF METHODOLOGICAL CONSENSUS prevented generalising the performance parameters and produced contradictory results across studies. That is the reason two sound papers here can disagree without either being wrong, and it is the argument for recording where our sources conflict rather than picking a winner. Also notes that the ISB recommendations are rarely followed, and that the subjects are overwhelmingly male — read alongside ref.horan2010 and ref.zheng2008b before assuming any published figure applies to a woman.

references.title: Kinematic analysis of swing in pro and amateur golfers
references.establishes: 72 male golfers across four skill levels, optoelectronic capture at 240 Hz. Professionals reached larger ranges of motion at the top — left shoulder horizontal adduction 125±6°, right shoulder external rotation 66±11°, trunk rotation 60±7° — and the highest downswing angular velocities, club shaft 2413±442°/s with right elbow extension 854±150°/s and wrists near 1100°/s. The authors read the middle- and high-handicap patterns as improper mechanics that may contribute to injury. TREAT THAT LAST STEP CAREFULLY: the study measures kinematics, not injuries, so the injury link is the authors' inference and not a result — ref.watson2023 is the check on how far any such claim may be taken here.

references.title: Swing kinematics for male and female pro golfers
references.establishes: 25 LPGA and 25 PGA professionals, optoelectronic capture at 240 Hz. Finds sex differences at the professional level and locates them: trunk forward tilt at the top (25±4° vs 31±4°), pelvis orientation at the top (49±8° vs 42±7°), pelvis rotation at impact (-52±11° vs -42±12°), and lower angular velocities for the LPGA group at the club shaft, both wrists and elbow extension. The authors' emphasis is DISTAL — 'major differences were found at the wrist and elbow'. Note what is NOT in its list of significant differences: trunk axial rotation. COMPARE ref.horan2010, which finds the differences predominantly PROXIMAL — thorax and pelvis lateral and anterior-posterior tilt — and does report less axial rotation to the left in males at ball contact. The two agree that a woman's swing is not a man's; they disagree on where that shows and on axial rotation specifically. Both bear on whether the cohort work in norms.json should carry a sex axis, and neither settles it alone.

references.title: Thorax and pelvis kinematics during the downswing of male and female skilled golfers
references.establishes: 19 male and 19 female skilled golfers (handicap ≤4), optical capture, 3D thorax and pelvis profiles across the WHOLE downswing rather than at the top and impact alone — which is its methodological point: most of the literature samples two instants and cannot see the coordination between them. At ball contact males showed greater pelvis posterior tilt, greater pelvis and thorax lateral tilt to the right, and LESS axial rotation to the left than females, plus greater peak angular velocities in tilt. Concludes that what is considered optimal for male golfers should not be generalised to female golfers. COMPARE ref.zheng2008b: both find sex differences, but Zheng locates the major ones distally at the wrist and elbow and does not report a significant trunk axial-rotation difference, where this study finds the differences proximally in tilt and does report one in axial rotation. Read together before any norm is split, or not split, on sex.

references.title: Assessment of planarity of the golf swing based on the functional swing plane of the clubhead and motion planes of the body points
references.establishes: 14 skilled male golfers (mean handicap -0.5±2.0), three clubs, optical capture at 250 Hz. The load-bearing result for anyone drawing a plane on a video: the downswing is SEMI-planar, not planar. Skilled golfers hold a well-defined functional swing plane for the clubhead and well-defined motion planes for the shoulder and arm points, but those planes are vastly different from one another and the points deviate substantially from the clubhead's plane. The downswing separates into a transition phase and a planar execution phase, and only the second is plane-like. Slope and direction of the functional plane show a significant club effect (p<0.001), so 'the swing plane' is not one plane per golfer either. Read with ref.madrid2020, which measures on-plane angular motions of the axle-chain system against clubhead speed; neither treats a single plane as settled.

references.title: A three dimensional kinematic and kinetic study of the golf swing
references.journal: Journal of Sports Science and Medicine
references.establishes: 85 amateur golfers (84 male) spanning a wide skill range, driven through a full-body model coupled to a FLEXIBLE club model — the kinetic counterpart to the kinematic studies here, giving forces, torques, work and power alongside trajectories and shaft deflection. Two findings carry: the wrists dominate the generation of clubhead velocity and the orientation of the face, and the variables correlating most strongly with skill are the HAND TRAJECTORY and work capacity rather than any single joint angle. It also records how individually variable the swing is between subjects, which is a caution against reading any of these means as a template. This journal issues no DOI, so the PMID is the identifier.

references.title: The lumbar spine and low back pain in golf: a literature review of swing biomechanics and injury prevention
references.establishes: Review of lumbar loading in the swing, the modern versus classic technique argument, and what the evidence supports doing about it. Reports that physical therapy targeting transversus abdominis and multifidus is central to managing low back pain, and that classic-swing coaching plus improved trunk flexibility MAY add to it. Its most honest passage is the gap it names: almost no study separates the effect of a swing modification from the effect of the rehabilitation delivered alongside it, so controlled trials are still needed before any swing change can be claimed to reduce pain. It argues for individualised intervention over a universal protocol. Read as the older survey behind ref.edwards2020 and ref.cole2016, and bounded by ref.watson2023 — nothing here licenses telling a golfer that a swing change will fix their back.

references.title: The Search for the Perfect Swing
references.establishes: The book the scientific study of the golf swing starts from: a multi-year programme of measurement commissioned by the Golf Society of Great Britain, covering swing mechanics as a double pendulum, impact, ball flight, and the statistics of scoring. Its lasting contribution is methodological — it is the first sustained attempt to decide golf questions by measurement rather than by authority, and most of the quantities this product computes descend from questions it framed. GENERAL READING, not support: it predates every instrument here, its figures have been superseded in detail, and an ISBN-only record cannot back a peer tier in any case. First published 1968; the ISBN identifies the Triumph Books reissue.

references.title: The Physics of Golf
references.establishes: A physicist's book-length treatment of the swing as a mechanical system — the double-pendulum model worked through properly, with the release of the wrist cock, the energy transfer to the clubhead, shaft behaviour and the impact interval each derived rather than asserted. The companion volume to ref.penner2003, which is the peer-reviewed review of much the same ground: read the paper for what the field accepts, this for the derivations behind it. Useful here as the reasoning behind the wrist-release and clubhead-speed claims the library makes, and it is reasoning rather than evidence — the models are analytic, and the golfers in them are idealised.

references.title: Five Lessons: The Modern Fundamentals of Golf
references.establishes: The most widely taught instruction text in the game, and the origin of a large share of the vocabulary this library records at the `practice` tier — the grip, the plane of glass through the shoulders, the waggle, and the sequencing of the downswing from the lower body. It is here so that 'the field agrees and has never measured it' can finally name the field: many conditions in this pack describe faults defined against what this book prescribes. INSTRUCTION, NOT EVIDENCE. It reports one exceptional player's account of his own method, contains no measurement, and cannot back `supported` or `established` — the loader enforces that. Where it disagrees with a measured source, the measured source wins. First published 1957; the ISBN identifies the Pocket Books edition.

references.title: Golf My Way
references.establishes: The other pillar of the modern instruction canon alongside ref.hogan1957, and a deliberately different one: where Hogan prescribes a method, this describes a method and repeatedly says which parts are personal to its author. That distinction is worth having in the registry, because a `practice`-tier claim sourced here is weaker than the same claim sourced from a text that claims universality — and stronger in a different way, since it admits its own scope. Same limit as every instruction text: one player's account, no measurement, and it may not back a peer tier.

references.title: The Golf Swing
references.establishes: The teaching text that carried the modern-swing model — connection, a stable lower body, the body-driven rather than hands-driven downswing — into mainstream coaching, and the source of much of the fault vocabulary a coach will use with this product's output. Recorded here because the library must be able to say WHOSE model a `practice` claim reflects; several conditions in this pack are faults only relative to this model and would not be faults relative to ref.nicklaus1974. Instruction, not measurement: it may not back a peer tier, and where it and ref.gluck2008 disagree about what the modern swing costs the lumbar spine, the review is the one with evidence behind it.

references.title: The Golfing Machine
references.establishes: The most systematic attempt to describe the swing as geometry rather than as advice — an enumerated catalogue of components and their permissible combinations, written by an engineer and the origin of terms a coach may well use in front of this product's output. Its value here is that it is FALSIFIABLE in a way instruction texts usually are not: it makes geometric claims that measurement can check, and ref.kwon2012's finding that the downswing is only semi-planar is exactly such a check. NOTE THE PUBLISHER: Star System Press is the imprint of the commercial instruction system of the same name as the book. The TEXT is common domain and is recorded; the system's instructor programme is an attribution this repo does not carry, and must not be named anywhere in the content. Original edition 1979; the ISBN identifies a Star System Press printing.
